blocks.text: A pacemaker is an electronic medical device that delivers electrical impulses to the heart to initiate or regulate cardiac contractions when the heart's natural electrical conduction system cannot maintain an adequate heart rate or rhythm.
Pacemakers are used primarily to treat clinically significant bradycardia and certain conduction disorders.
Unlike a cardiac monitor, which detects and displays cardiac electrical activity, a pacemaker can actively stimulate the heart.

items.text: Category: Cardiovascular therapeutic equipment.
Type: Electronic cardiac stimulation device.
Function: Electrical stimulation of the myocardium.
Common indications: Symptomatic bradycardia and selected conduction abnormalities.
Types: Temporary and permanent pacemakers.

blocks.text: A. Permanent pacemaker
Implanted under the skin, commonly in the upper chest, with leads positioned in the heart when a lead-based system is used. It provides long-term treatment for selected rhythm disorders.
B. Temporary transvenous pacemaker
An external pulse generator delivers impulses through a pacing catheter inserted into the heart through a vein. It is used for temporary support when clinically indicated.
C. Temporary transcutaneous pacemaker
Delivers electrical impulses through large adhesive pads on the chest and back. It can provide emergency pacing while definitive management is arranged.
D. Leadless pacemaker
A small device implanted directly inside the heart, avoiding conventional transvenous pacing leads. It is suitable for selected patients.

"This is a cardiac pacemaker, an electronic device that delivers electrical impulses to stimulate the myocardium and maintain an appropriate heart rate. It may be temporary or permanent and is used mainly in patients with symptomatic bradycardia or clinically significant conduction disorders."

Examiner tip: State the distinction between a pacemaker and a defibrillator. A pacemaker primarily treats slow rhythms, whereas a defibrillator can deliver shocks to treat selected life-threatening tachyarrhythmias.
The principal role of a pacemaker is to prevent an excessively slow heart rate or inadequate cardiac activation caused by abnormalities in impulse formation or conduction.
A pacemaker may be indicated when a slow heart rate causes symptoms such as:

items.text: Syncope.
Presyncope.
Dizziness.
Exercise intolerance.
Fatigue.
Heart failure symptoms attributable to bradycardia.

blocks.text: The decision depends on the rhythm diagnosis and clinical context, not on heart rate alone.

blocks.title: Permanent pacing is commonly indicated for:

items.text: Acquired Mobitz type II second-degree AV block.
High-grade AV block.
Complete (third-degree) AV block.

blocks.text: These indications generally apply when the conduction abnormality is not due to a reversible or physiological cause.

items.text: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia.
Symptomatic sinus pauses.
Tachycardia–bradycardia syndrome.
Inability to increase heart rate appropriately with activity when symptoms are attributable to chronotropic incompetence.
Certain neuromuscular disorders associated with progressive conduction disease.
Selected reflex syncope cases with documented cardioinhibitory mechanisms.
Cardiac resynchronization therapy in selected patients with heart failure and electrical dyssynchrony.

blocks.text: Important: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is a specialized pacing therapy for selected heart failure patients, not simply treatment for a slow heart rate.

blocks.title: Temporary pacing may be required for selected patients with:

items.text: Hemodynamically significant bradycardia unresponsive to initial treatment.
Advanced AV block requiring urgent support.
Bradycardia due to a potentially reversible cause while the underlying problem is treated.
Selected situations around cardiac procedures.

blocks.text: Temporary pacing is not required for every case of bradycardia or every episode of heart block. The patient's stability, rhythm, cause, and response to treatment guide management.

blocks.text: A leadless pacemaker has its pacing electronics and electrode integrated into a small intracardiac device. It does not use the conventional pulse-generator-and-transvenous-lead arrangement.
Single-chamber pacemaker
Typically stimulates the right atrium or right ventricle, depending on the indication and device design.
Dual-chamber pacemaker
Uses atrial and ventricular leads to coordinate atrial and ventricular activity when appropriate.
Biventricular pacemaker (CRT-P)
Coordinates ventricular activation in selected patients with heart failure and electrical dyssynchrony.

blocks.title: The first three positions of the traditional NBG pacemaker code describe:

items.text: First position: Chamber paced.
Second position: Chamber sensed.
Third position: Response to sensing.
A — Atrium.
V — Ventricle.
D — Dual chamber.
O — None.
I — Inhibited response.
T — Triggered response.

blocks.text: For example, VVI means ventricular pacing, ventricular sensing, and inhibition of pacing when an appropriate intrinsic ventricular event is sensed.
DDD indicates dual-chamber pacing and sensing with a dual response to sensed events.

items.text: Prevents symptomatic bradycardia: Maintains an adequate heart rate when intrinsic cardiac activity is insufficient.
Improves symptoms: May reduce syncope, dizziness, fatigue, and exercise intolerance caused by bradycardia.
Improves AV synchrony: Selected dual-chamber systems coordinate atrial and ventricular activity.
Provides long-term support: Permanent devices can function for years, depending on the device, settings, and battery usage.
Can improve quality of life: Particularly when symptoms are directly attributable to a pacing-responsive rhythm disorder.
Specialized pacing options: CRT can improve cardiac coordination in appropriately selected heart failure patients.
Programmable operation: Clinicians can adjust pacing parameters to suit the patient's clinical needs.
Invasive implantation: Conventional permanent pacing usually requires a procedure.
Infection risk: Infection may involve the generator pocket, leads, or bloodstream.
Lead-related complications: Lead displacement, fracture, insulation failure, or abnormal sensing may occur.
Battery depletion: Generator replacement is eventually required.
Device dependence: Some patients rely heavily on pacing, making device malfunction potentially dangerous.
Not a cure for every arrhythmia: A conventional pacemaker does not treat all causes of syncope, tachycardia, or cardiac arrest.
Follow-up required: Patients need device checks and clinical review.
Potential electromagnetic interference: Certain equipment and procedures require specific precautions.
Pacing-induced ventricular dysfunction: Chronic right ventricular pacing can impair ventricular function in some patients.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: A pacemaker can maintain heart rate, but it does not automatically restore normal cardiac output if the patient has severe myocardial dysfunction, hypovolemia, or another cause of shock.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to Use It — Step-by-Step OSCE Demonstration

blocks.text: For an OSCE, you may be asked to identify a pacemaker, explain its operation, inspect a patient with an implanted device, or demonstrate emergency transcutaneous pacing.

content_groups.group_title: Station A: Identifying and explaining a pacemaker

blocks.text: bhf.org.uk
Step 1: Identify the device
State that it is a cardiac pacemaker and distinguish permanent from temporary pacing equipment where possible.
Step 2: Explain the function
Describe how the device senses intrinsic cardiac activity and delivers electrical impulses when required by its programmed settings.
Step 3: Identify the components
Point out the pulse generator, battery, lead or leads, and electrode tips where visible.
Step 4: State the indications
Mention symptomatic bradycardia, advanced AV block, and selected cases of sinus node dysfunction.
Step 5: Explain monitoring and follow-up
Describe ECG assessment, device interrogation, wound review after implantation, and ongoing follow-up.
This is a time-critical intervention for selected patients with clinically significant bradycardia.

items.text: Assess the patient and activate appropriate emergency support.
Confirm the indication for pacing and follow the applicable resuscitation algorithm.
Attach ECG monitoring and apply pacing pads correctly.
Select the pacing mode and set the initial rate and output according to the device and clinical protocol.
Increase output as required until electrical capture is obtained.
Confirm mechanical capture by assessing a corresponding pulse and clinical perfusion.
Reassess blood pressure, consciousness, and overall clinical response.
Provide analgesia or sedation when appropriate without delaying urgent treatment.
Arrange expert review and definitive management, including transvenous pacing when indicated.

blocks.text: Critical OSCE point: Electrical capture alone does not prove that the heart is producing an effective pulse. Always confirm mechanical capture.

content_groups.group_title: Station C: Assessing a patient with an implanted pacemaker

items.text: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs.
Ask about syncope, dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, or breathlessness.
Inspect the device pocket for redness, swelling, discharge, or erosion.
Obtain a 12-lead ECG when indicated.
Check for pacing spikes, capture, and relevant rhythm abnormalities.
Arrange pacemaker interrogation if malfunction is suspected.
Escalate urgently if the patient is unstable or device failure is suspected.

blocks.text: There is no single absolute contraindication that applies to every pacemaker system and every clinical situation.

items.text: A permanent pacemaker should not be implanted without a valid clinical indication.
Reversible causes of bradycardia should be assessed and treated when appropriate.
Active infection requires careful management and may necessitate delaying permanent implantation when clinically feasible.
Temporary pacing should be used when its expected benefit outweighs the procedural risks.
Device selection must account for the patient's rhythm disorder, anatomy, comorbidities, and expected pacing requirements.

blocks.text: Failure to capture
Pacing spikes occur, but the expected atrial depolarization or ventricular QRS complex does not follow.
Failure to pace
The device fails to deliver a pacing impulse when one is expected.
Sensing abnormality
The device incorrectly detects or fails to detect intrinsic electrical activity, causing inappropriate pacing behaviour.
Clinical safety: Suspected pacemaker malfunction in an unstable patient requires immediate assessment and emergency support. Do not delay treatment while waiting for routine device interrogation.
A functioning pacemaker should demonstrate appropriate sensing, pacing when required, and capture when an impulse is delivered.

blocks.title: On ECG, expected findings may include:

Pacing spikes before a QRS complex in ventricular pacing.
A paced QRS complex following ventricular pacing, often broad in conventional right ventricular pacing.
Appropriate intrinsic cardiac activity when the pacemaker does not need to stimulate.
Appropriate coordination of atrial and ventricular events in dual-chamber pacing when programmed and functioning normally.

blocks.text: Important: A normal pacemaker does not need to produce a pacing spike before every heartbeat. Many devices are demand pacemakers that allow intrinsic activity when it is adequate.

content_groups.group_title: C. Pacemaker spikes: what to remember

blocks.text: A pacing spike is a brief electrical deflection representing delivery of a pacing impulse.
For ventricular pacing, successful capture is generally demonstrated by a QRS complex following the pacing spike. For atrial pacing, a P wave should follow.
However, not all devices produce clearly visible spikes on every ECG recording, and interpretation must account for the device's programmed settings.

Congenital heart disease: Abnormal cardiac anatomy may affect device and lead selection.
Growth: A child's growth can affect lead requirements and long-term device planning.
Skin and tissue: Smaller body size requires careful consideration of generator position and wound healing.
Battery longevity: Pacing settings, lead characteristics, and growth-related factors influence long-term device management.
Activity: Advice should be individualized to the device, procedure, and underlying cardiac condition.

blocks.text: Permanent pacing may be indicated in congenital complete AV block when there are symptoms, ventricular dysfunction, a wide QRS escape rhythm, or other recognized risk factors. Some asymptomatic children also meet pacing criteria depending on their ventricular rate and clinical findings.

OSCE pearl: In children, the decision to implant a pacemaker is based on the underlying condition, symptoms, rhythm characteristics, and evidence of cardiac compromise—not simply on an adult heart-rate threshold.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE Questions and Model Answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a pacemaker?
An electronic device that delivers electrical impulses to stimulate the heart when intrinsic impulse formation or conduction is inadequate.
Q2. What are the major indications for permanent pacing?
Common indications include symptomatic sinus node dysfunction, acquired Mobitz type II AV block, high-grade AV block, and complete AV block when not due to a reversible or physiological cause.
Q3. What is the difference between temporary and permanent pacing?

Temporary pacing provides short-term support using an external generator and a transcutaneous or transvenous pacing system. Permanent pacing involves an implanted device intended for long-term treatment.
Q4. What is a demand pacemaker?
A demand pacemaker senses intrinsic cardiac activity and delivers pacing impulses when needed according to its programmed parameters.
Q5. What is failure to capture?
It occurs when a pacing impulse is delivered but fails to produce the expected myocardial depolarization.
Q6. What is failure to sense?
It occurs when the pacemaker fails to detect intrinsic cardiac electrical activity appropriately, potentially resulting in inappropriate pacing.
Q7. What is the difference between a pacemaker and a defibrillator?
A conventional pacemaker primarily treats bradyarrhythmias. An ICD can detect and treat selected life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias using antitachycardia pacing or electrical shocks.
Q8. What is the purpose of dual-chamber pacing?
It allows sensing and pacing in both the atrium and ventricle, facilitating coordination between atrial and ventricular activity when appropriate.
Q9. What complications can follow pacemaker implantation?
Infection, hematoma, pneumothorax, lead displacement, lead damage, cardiac perforation, and device malfunction are important complications.
Q10. How do you confirm mechanical capture during transcutaneous pacing?
Assess for a corresponding palpable pulse, improvement in perfusion, and appropriate hemodynamic response. Electrical capture on ECG alone is insufficient.
Q11. Can a patient with a pacemaker undergo MRI?
Many patients can undergo MRI under an appropriate protocol, but device and lead compatibility, programming, monitoring, and specialist review must be confirmed beforehand.
Q12. What should you do if a patient with a pacemaker collapses?

Assess responsiveness, breathing, and circulation; activate emergency support; and follow the appropriate resuscitation algorithm. Evaluate the rhythm and possible device malfunction without delaying lifesaving interventions.
Q13. What is pacemaker syndrome?

A collection of symptoms caused by adverse haemodynamic effects of inappropriate atrioventricular timing or loss of AV synchrony, including dizziness, fatigue, hypotension, and sometimes neck pulsations.
Q14. What does VVI mean?
Ventricular pacing, ventricular sensing, and inhibition of pacing in response to an appropriately sensed intrinsic ventricular event.

blocks.text: "This is a cardiac pacemaker, an electronic device that delivers electrical impulses to stimulate the heart when intrinsic cardiac activity is inadequate.
